title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity. title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces. The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution.

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests.

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. text: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.
